En avril dernier, alors que j’étais à la: Last April, while I was hosting the daily show Les aurores Montréal on CIBL 101.5 FM, I had the chance to speak on air with Marjorie Villefranche just after she had announced her retirement. When I joined La Converse, I soon realized that her departure had received very little media coverage, so I suggested writing an article about her.
Comme Marjorie Villefranche a été la dir: Because Marjorie Villefranche was the executive director of an organization at the heart of life for newcomers, particularly Haitian ones, it seemed essential to me to write a profile that would highlight her 40 years of community engagement and activism.
M<sup>me</sup> Villefranche ayant décidé: Since M<sup>s</sup>. Villefranche had decided to begin her retirement on another continent, our reunion unfortunately took place behind a screen. As this is my first feature article for La Converse, I questioned myself a little more often than any good journalist would.
Le 11 août 2025, l’ancienne directrice g: On August 11, 2025, the former executive director of Maison d’Haïti, Marjorie Villefranche, joins us from the other side of the Atlantic. Freshly retired, she has flown to France, where she will spend the next two months. Behind her screen, she is smiling, her red glasses firmly in place. She expresses a certain nostalgia for her years at Maison d’Haïti.
Marjorie Villefranche en a été la direct: Marjorie Villefranche was its executive director from 2011 to April 2025. After 14 years at the helm of the organization, she has just passed the torch to Arcelle Appolon.
Fondé en 1973, l’organisme est un repère: Founded in 1973, the organization is an essential landmark for immigrants and refugees arriving from Haiti. Over the decades, it has grown into a welcoming space open to all newcomers in the Saint-Michel neighbourhood.
Née en Haïti, Marjorie Villefranche a qu: Born in Haiti, Marjorie Villefranche left the country with her brother to flee the Duvalier dictatorship and settled in Quebec in 1964. Exile to Quebec became a necessity, as her childhood already bore the painful marks of her mother’s arbitrary arrest; she was imprisoned and beaten by the regime.
La Maison d’Haïti s’inscrit profondément: Maison d’Haïti is deeply woven into her story: she first walked through its doors in 1975, became an employee eight years later, then took over as executive director in 2011. Embracing her dual identity as both Haitian and Quebecer, she tells us that it was through the organization that she came to understand Haitian culture.
« Ma culture haïtienne, je ne la connais: “I didn’t know my Haitian culture, because I left when I was 12. […] I first went to Maison d’Haïti not to work there, but to take part in the activities and discover my roots,” she says softly.
Paradoxalement, c’est lorsqu’elle est dé: Paradoxically, it was once she was already settled in Quebec that she immersed herself in Haitian culture: “I think it’s an organization that saved my life!” she exclaims. “When I was young, I wasn’t at peace with myself. It was only at Maison d’Haïti that I was able to reconcile with who I was, by understanding that piece of myself that I couldn’t grasp anywhere else.”
<strong>Ne laisser tomber personne</stro: Letting no one fall through the cracks
Nous l’interrogeons sur son souvenir le: We ask her about the most memorable moment of her career at Maison d’Haïti. It is a loaded question for a woman whose path has been intertwined with the history of this institution since 1983. She thinks, then without hesitation names the earthquake of January 12, 2010, the moment when everything changed for Haitian communities here and elsewhere.
Un puissant séisme de magnitude 7,0 à 7,: A powerful earthquake of magnitude 7.0 to 7.3 strikes Haiti. The strongest tremor lasts 30 seconds. In the blink of an eye, the capital and its surroundings are devastated. Countless buildings and structures are destroyed, and the cathedral of Port-au-Prince is levelled.
Le bilan humain de la catastrophe est dr: The human toll of the disaster is staggering: <l1>280,000 dead, 300,000 injured and 1.3 million homeless</l1>.
À ce jour, ce séisme demeure l’un des pl: To this day, the earthquake remains one of the deadliest in modern history.
« On ne connaissait pas notre capacité à: “We didn’t know our capacity to respond to a disaster. It was a revelation for us to succeed in helping hundreds of people who were grieving… to welcome the people who were coming from Haiti too […] but above all to fight for the immigration file under the [Canadian] Conservative government of the time, which didn’t want a special program for Haitians, despite the earthquake.”
Au fil des décennies, la Maison d’Haïti: Over the decades, Maison d’Haïti has lived through the difficult and decisive periods of the Pearl of the Antilles. The organization came into being in 1972, during a major migration movement caused by the authoritarian regime of Jean-Claude Duvalier, known as “Baby Doc,” who had taken power a year earlier, succeeding his father, François Duvalier, known as “Papa Doc.”
Avant le tremblement de terre de 2010, l: Before the 2010 earthquake, Maison d’Haïti lived through the fall of the Duvalier dictatorship in 1986, the AIDS crisis that had erupted four years earlier – and the stigma it cast on Haitian people, wrongly declared by the Red Cross to be at higher risk of carrying the virus. The 1991 coup d’état against President Jean-Bertrand Aristide followed, among other events. Today, the organization faces a country fractured by gang violence as well as the recent<l1> rise in asylum claims,</l1> a consequence of the new Trump-era immigration policies.
À travers toutes ces épreuves, M<sup>me<: Through all these trials, M<sup>s</sup>. Villefranche has remained faithful to a principle that is deeply important to her: “Let no one fall through the cracks,” she says, speaking of the people who use Maison d’Haïti’s services.
La septuagénaire se dit partagée à l’idé: The septuagenarian says she feels torn about passing the torch. Although she is taking a well-deserved retirement and personally guided M<sup>s</sup>. Apollon through her transition, detaching herself from this institution, which she carried and defended for over a decade, is still a major turning point in her life. “I was more sad than happy. It’s as if something was being torn away from me. On the one hand, I’m happy because I’m leaving with a serene mind. The person replacing me is a good person. But I didn’t think I would feel such sadness.”
Lorsqu’on lui demande quels conseils ell: Asked what advice she has to ensure the organization’s longevity, now that she has bowed out, she answers: “Don’t get caught up in the anecdotal and don’t lose sight of our role. We’re here to help people and defend their rights. We’re here and not elsewhere.”
Sur place, à la Maison d’Haïti, Arcelle: At Maison d’Haïti, Arcelle Appolon, the new director, sits with her glasses in her hands. Her turquoise shirt blends harmoniously with the filing cabinet of the same shade behind her. Her braided hair is pulled up in a bun. Smiling, she is ready to answer our questions.

Lorsqu’on l’invite à réagir aux propos d: Invited to react to her predecessor’s remarks, she answers without hesitation: “I can hardly see how anyone could not take advice from Marjorie Villefranche. As a woman, as a woman from an ethnocultural minority, as a woman involved in her community, any advice from her is welcome.”
Elle lui donne raison, insistant sur le: She agrees with her, stressing that we must not forget “who” the organization works for. Community organizing exists to serve human beings, she insists.
Sa voix se fait plus vive, et son regard: Her voice grows livelier, her gaze more expressive. “When we talk about immigration, we’re talking about human beings who, often for reasons beyond their control, are forced to make the difficult choice of leaving the place where they live. […] We make the mistake of thinking that everyone dreams of living in Canada. No, everyone dreams of escaping what’s happening in their country.”
En pesant ses mots, M<sup>me</sup> Ville: Choosing her words carefully, M<sup>s</sup>. Villefranche goes on to say that one of Maison d’Haïti’s most pressing missions right now is helping people with the steps to bring over their loved ones, or to regularize their own immigration status after arriving from the United States. Deadlines are tight, as short as 24 days. Each declaration must be completed carefully, because it will serve as the basis for the government’s assessment, the former director stresses.
Sa voix s’anime : « Il faut comprendre q: Her voice becomes animated: “You have to understand that when we talk about asylum seekers or immigrants, we seem to forget that they aren’t only adults. Nearly 40% are children. We must never lose sight of that.”
Elle évoque alors des cas de déchirement: She then describes cases of families torn apart at the border where, for example, only the father, who has relatives in Canada, can file a refugee claim. The decision rests with immigration officers: “‘You, sir, can come in with the children; madam, who has no ties here, has to go back to the United States,’” she says as an example.
Elle met alors des mots sur un drame sil: She then puts words to a silent but very real tragedy: “Children in tears, unable to sleep, wondering why their mother was torn away from them.”
<strong>Le Québec, une terre d’accueil e: Quebec, a land of welcome on the verge of disappearing?
En avril 2025, le premier ministre du Qu: In April 2025, Quebec Premier François Legault stated that the province had reached<l1> its maximum capacity to take in</l1> new immigrants because of the large number of asylum seekers, mainly of Haitian origin.
M<sup>mes</sup> Villefranche et Appolon: M<sup>s</sup>. Villefranche and Ms. Appolon react to these remarks. The former doesn’t mince words. “It’s an extremely hypocritical stance, because today the Chamber of Commerce is saying we need 100,000 immigrants a year,” she says.
La retraitée fait ici référence aux prop: The retiree is referring to statements by the Fédération des chambres de commerce du Québec (FCCQ), which said on August 11 that the province will need to welcome<l1> more than 100,000 immigrants a year by 2029</l1> to meet the current needs of the labour market. The finding is based on data from the ministère de l’Emploi.
« Voilà des familles qui n’[immigrent] p: “These are families who aren’t [immigrating] for fun. They’re trying not to die. To answer that the yard is full… full of what? Ill will, quite simply,” adds the former director. M<sup>s</sup>. Villefranche immediately recalls the special program set up for Ukrainians, under which 100,000 visas were issued. “Why wouldn’t we create a special program for Haitians?” she asks. As for the capacity of the Belle Province to take in asylum seekers, she notes that they must have family here in order to file a claim. For her, the rise in asylum claims concerns families more than the province.
À l’idée de succéder à une figure emblém: On succeeding an emblematic figure of the community sector, Ms. Appolon adds that she approaches it all “with humility.” Going forward, she says, we should ask ourselves: “What do I have in my djakout* that I can bring […] to the vision of those who came before me?”
Son cheval de bataille est le financemen: Her main cause is funding. She admits she has to cut three programs previously offered by Maison d’Haïti for now, for lack of resources. One of them is Le Projet Gars, which aimed to raise awareness about toxic masculinity and was dedicated to boys from Haitian communities.
Dans le contexte actuel, la Maison d’Haï: In the current context, Maison d’Haïti is very busy, as we saw during our visit, when about thirty people, including asylum seekers, were there to ask for support.
M<sup>me</sup> Villefranche tient à rapp: M<sup>s</sup>. Villefranche wants to remind people that Canada has benefited enormously from the contributions of the Haitian community. The founders of Maison d’Haïti, Adeline and Max Chancy, were part of the first wave of Haitian migrants to Quebec, known as the “brain drain.” This movement, which took place in 1965 as people fled the dictatorship of Duvalier père, was given that name because the migrants who were part of it were highly educated. The Chancys’ contribution to Quebec society illustrates the kind of contribution M<sup>s</sup>. Villefranche is referring to. From Chancy to Appolon, the latter sees the former executive director’s legacy as “a strong legacy, a rich legacy, a legacy that we collectively have a responsibility to carry forward,” speaking of Marjorie Villefranche’s many decades of community involvement and activism.
